learning_objective: 🎯 Turn boring numbers into beautiful visuals! Learn how to draw diagrams and thematic maps to make geographic data pop.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Line graphs show trends over time (like temperature). Bar diagrams show comparisons (like crop production). Polygraphs show multiple line graphs on one chart.
A circle divided into sectors, representing percentages or proportions of a total (e.g., land use showing 30% forest, 50% agriculture). Based on 360 degrees.
Maps that use shades of a single color or different patterns to show data distribution across regions (e.g., dark red for high population density, light pink for low).
Using identical dots to represent the exact number and distribution of something (e.g., 1 dot = 10,000 people). Excellent for showing concentration and dispersion.
Maps using imaginary lines connecting places of equal value. Isobars connect equal air pressure, Isotherms connect equal temperature, and Contours connect equal elevation.

fun_activity.title: 🍕 The Day Pie
fun_activity.instructions: Draw a circle. Divide your 24-hour day into a pie chart. If you sleep 8 hours, that is 1/3rd of the pie (120 degrees)! Color code sleep, school, play, and study.

exam_tips: 📌 Know the formula for converting percentages to degrees for a Pie Chart: (Value ÷ Total Value) × 360.
📌 Always include a legend/key, scale, and title when drawing thematic maps.
📌 Remember: Dot maps show distribution, while Choropleth maps are best for showing density or rates.
quick_recap: ⭐ The star diagram is used to represent the frequency of wind directions.
⭐ Thematic maps tell a specific story, unlike physical maps which just show geography.
⭐ Isopleths do not respect administrative boundaries; they follow the data naturally.
